checks.title: EBS encryption by default is enabled in every region with EC2 instances

verify.pass_when_text: The instance's region has EbsEncryptionByDefault=true. It is a per-region test, like Drata's 218 and Vanta's: if the setting is off, every instance in that region is reported and a single command resolves it. With no EC2 instances there is nothing to evaluate. The setting does not encrypt volumes that already exist (see ENC-002).

vanta.test: EBS volume encryption is enabled in all regions

steps: Turn on EBS encryption by default in region {region}; it affects only the volumes and snapshots created from now on.
Verify with get-ebs-encryption-by-default and, to encrypt the volumes that already exist, follow ENC-002.
commands:
REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
aws ec2 enable-ebs-encryption-by-default --region "$REGION"
remediation.notes: No downtime. It uses the aws/ebs key; for your own CMK, aws ec2 modify-ebs-default-kms-key-id --kms-key-id <key> in the same region. The setting is per region: repeat it in every region that has instances. It does not encrypt existing volumes.

verify.offenders: Volumes[?Encrypted!=`true`].{resource_id: VolumeId, detail: {State: State, Size: Size, VolumeType: VolumeType, Instances: Attachments[].InstanceId}}
verify.pass_when_text: All volumes have Encrypted=true. An unencrypted volume cannot be encrypted in place: it must be replaced with an encrypted copy.

steps: Turn on default encryption first (ENC-001) so that new volumes are born encrypted.
Choose the KMS key (alias/aws/ebs or your own CMK) and a maintenance window: the instance that owns volume {resource_id} is stopped.
Stop the instance and wait for it to be stopped BEFORE the snapshot (first block): that way later writes are not lost. An unattached volume does not need this step.

Create a snapshot of volume {resource_id}, copy it with encryption and create a new volume from the copy in the same Availability Zone (second block; it stops with STOPPED if the instance is still running).
Replace the old volume with the encrypted one on the same device and start the instance (third block).
Verify that the instance boots with its data and only then delete the unencrypted volume and snapshots (by hand, there is no command for that).
commands:
REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
INSTANCE_ID="__FILL_IN_INSTANCE_ID__"
# stops the instance that owns the volume BEFORE the snapshot, so that later writes are not lost: downtime until the start-instances of the third block
aws ec2 stop-instances --instance-ids "$INSTANCE_ID" --region "$REGION" && aws ec2 wait instance-stopped --instance-ids "$INSTANCE_ID" --region "$REGION"

REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
VOLUME_ID="{resource_id}"
KMS_KEY_ID="__FILL_IN_KMS_KEY_ID__"
AZ="__FILL_IN_AVAILABILITY_ZONE__"
# type, IOPS and throughput of the original volume (read-only); IOPS and throughput stay empty if the type does not use them
VOL_TYPE=$(aws ec2 describe-volumes --volume-ids "$VOLUME_ID" --region "$REGION" --query 'Volumes[0].VolumeType' --output text)
VOL_IOPS=$(aws ec2 describe-volumes --volume-ids "$VOLUME_ID" --region "$REGION" --query 'Volumes[0].Iops' --output text)
VOL_THROUGHPUT=$(aws ec2 describe-volumes --volume-ids "$VOLUME_ID" --region "$REGION" --query 'Volumes[0].Throughput' --output text)
IOPS_ARG=""; case "$VOL_TYPE" in gp3|io1|io2) [ "$VOL_IOPS" != "None" ] && IOPS_ARG="--iops $VOL_IOPS";; esac
THR_ARG=""; [ "$VOL_TYPE" = "gp3" ] && [ "$VOL_THROUGHPUT" != "None" ] && THR_ARG="--throughput $VOL_THROUGHPUT"
# the owning instance must be stopped before the snapshot (otherwise later writes are lost); an unattached volume does not need it
ATTACHED_TO=$(aws ec2 describe-volumes --volume-ids "$VOLUME_ID" --region "$REGION" --query 'Volumes[0].Attachments[0].InstanceId' --output text)
INSTANCE_STATE="stopped"
[ "$ATTACHED_TO" != "None" ] && INSTANCE_STATE=$(aws ec2 describe-instances --instance-ids "$ATTACHED_TO" --region "$REGION" --query 'Reservations[0].Instances[0].State.Name' --output text)
if [ "$INSTANCE_STATE" != "stopped" ]; then echo "STOPPED: instance $ATTACHED_TO is not stopped (state: $INSTANCE_STATE): stop it with the first block and wait for it to stop before taking the snapshot"; else
[ -n "$VOL_TYPE" ] && [ "$VOL_TYPE" != "None" ] && SNAP_ID=$(aws ec2 create-snapshot --volume-id "$VOLUME_ID" --region "$REGION" --query SnapshotId --output text) && aws ec2 wait snapshot-completed --snapshot-ids "$SNAP_ID" --region "$REGION" && ENC_SNAP_ID=$(aws ec2 copy-snapshot --source-region "$REGION" --source-snapshot-id "$SNAP_ID" --encrypted --kms-key-id "$KMS_KEY_ID" --region "$REGION" --query SnapshotId --output text) && aws ec2 wait snapshot-completed --snapshot-ids "$ENC_SNAP_ID" --region "$REGION" && aws ec2 create-volume --snapshot-id "$ENC_SNAP_ID" --availability-zone "$AZ" --volume-type "$VOL_TYPE" $IOPS_ARG $THR_ARG --region "$REGION" --query VolumeId --output text
fi

REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
INSTANCE_ID="__FILL_IN_INSTANCE_ID__"
OLD_VOLUME_ID="{resource_id}"
NEW_VOLUME_ID="__FILL_IN_ENCRYPTED_VOLUME_ID__"
DEVICE="__FILL_IN_DEVICE__"
# the instance is still stopped from the first block; the old volume stays detached, with the most recent data, until it is deleted by hand
aws ec2 wait instance-stopped --instance-ids "$INSTANCE_ID" --region "$REGION" && aws ec2 detach-volume --volume-id "$OLD_VOLUME_ID" --region "$REGION" && aws ec2 wait volume-available --volume-ids "$OLD_VOLUME_ID" --region "$REGION" && aws ec2 attach-volume --volume-id "$NEW_VOLUME_ID" --instance-id "$INSTANCE_ID" --device "$DEVICE" --region "$REGION" && aws ec2 start-instances --instance-ids "$INSTANCE_ID" --region "$REGION"
remediation.notes: WARNING: this is a replacement, not an in-place change, and it requires stopping the instance (downtime). The instance is stopped BEFORE the snapshot: if it were taken with the instance running, writes after the snapshot would not be on the new volume. The original volume is left detached with the most recent data until it is deleted by hand: keep it until the new one is validated. create-volume from an encrypted snapshot inherits the copy's encryption and key. For the root volume use the instance's root device (for example /dev/xvda). The new volume does not inherit DeleteOnTermination or the tags: reapply them. If the instance belongs to an Auto Scaling group, also fix the launch template (BlockDeviceMappings with Encrypted=true) and replace the instances. An unattached (available) volume is replaced without stopping anything. The new volume keeps the original's type, IOPS and throughput (read with describe-volumes). Data on instance store volumes is lost when the instance is stopped. Duplicated snapshots and volumes are billed until they are deleted.

checks.title: RDS instances and clusters have encrypted storage

verify.pass_when_text: Each instance and each cluster has StorageEncrypted=true. Instances that are members of a cluster (Aurora, Multi-AZ DB cluster) are evaluated through their cluster. RDS does not allow turning on encryption on an existing database: it must be restored from an encrypted snapshot.

vanta.test: Encryption at rest is enabled for RDS instances

steps: Choose the KMS key (aws/rds or your own CMK) and a maintenance window: the change replaces database {resource_id}. Write down its parameter group (DBParameterGroups or DBClusterParameterGroup) and, for an instance, its option group (OptionGroupMemberships): the blocks need them.

STOP APPLICATION WRITES before the snapshot (maintenance mode, or stop the services that write to the database) and keep them stopped until the switch to the new database: writes after the snapshot are lost. This is done at the application level, there is no command for it here.
Create a snapshot of the database and wait for it to be available.
Copy the snapshot with --kms-key-id to encrypt it and wait for the copy to be available.

Restore a new database from the encrypted copy with the same configuration (class, subnet group, security groups, parameter group and option group) and without public access (--no-publicly-accessible; if the original was public on purpose, decide that after restoring, never by omission). The first block is for an instance, the second one only for an Aurora cluster. Option groups are not inherited by restore-db-instance-from-db-snapshot: pass the original's (OPTION_GROUP).

Multi-AZ DB cluster (not Aurora; two readable standbys): do NOT use the second block (it is Aurora only). Restore the copied cluster snapshot with restore-db-cluster-from-snapshot passing --db-cluster-instance-class, --engine, the storage type and IOPS of the original, the subnet group, the security groups and the cluster parameter group: the restore creates the cluster's instances, so create-db-instance is not used. Plan it with the database owner.
Switch the application to the new database's endpoint (or rename the databases to keep the endpoint), start the application and verify that it works.
When everything works, delete the unencrypted database and the unencrypted snapshots.
commands:
REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
DB_ID="{resource_id}"
NEW_DB_ID="__FILL_IN_NEW_DB_ID__"
KMS_KEY_ID="__FILL_IN_KMS_KEY_ID__"
SUBNET_GROUP="__FILL_IN_DB_SUBNET_GROUP__"
SG_ID="__FILL_IN_SECURITY_GROUP_ID__"
PARAM_GROUP="__FILL_IN_PARAMETER_GROUP__"
OPTION_GROUP="__FILL_IN_OPTION_GROUP__"
# only for an instance that does not belong to a cluster. Run it AFTER stopping the application writes (second step). OPTION_GROUP is the original's option group (default:<engine>-<version> if it has no custom one); the new database is restored without public access (--no-publicly-accessible)
aws rds create-db-snapshot --db-instance-identifier "$DB_ID" --db-snapshot-identifier "$DB_ID-pre-encryption" --region "$REGION" && aws rds wait db-snapshot-available --db-snapshot-identifier "$DB_ID-pre-encryption" --region "$REGION" && aws rds copy-db-snapshot --source-db-snapshot-identifier "$DB_ID-pre-encryption" --target-db-snapshot-identifier "$DB_ID-encrypted" --kms-key-id "$KMS_KEY_ID" --region "$REGION" && aws rds wait db-snapshot-available --db-snapshot-identifier "$DB_ID-encrypted" --region "$REGION" && aws rds restore-db-instance-from-db-snapshot --db-instance-identifier "$NEW_DB_ID" --db-snapshot-identifier "$DB_ID-encrypted" --db-subnet-group-name "$SUBNET_GROUP" --vpc-security-group-ids "$SG_ID" --db-parameter-group-name "$PARAM_GROUP" --option-group-name "$OPTION_GROUP" --no-publicly-accessible --region "$REGION"

REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
CLUSTER_ID="{resource_id}"
NEW_CLUSTER_ID="__FILL_IN_NEW_CLUSTER_ID__"
KMS_KEY_ID="__FILL_IN_KMS_KEY_ID__"
SUBNET_GROUP="__FILL_IN_DB_SUBNET_GROUP__"
SG_ID="__FILL_IN_SECURITY_GROUP_ID__"
ENGINE="__FILL_IN_ENGINE__"
INSTANCE_CLASS="__FILL_IN_INSTANCE_CLASS__"
CLUSTER_PARAM_GROUP="__FILL_IN_CLUSTER_PARAMETER_GROUP__"
PARAM_GROUP="__FILL_IN_PARAMETER_GROUP__"
# AURORA ONLY (not for a Multi-AZ DB cluster: see the steps). Run it AFTER stopping the application writes (second step). The restored cluster comes with no instances, which is why create-db-instance at the end (without public access); both parameter groups are those of the original, otherwise the new cluster comes up with the default ones
aws rds create-db-cluster-snapshot --db-cluster-identifier "$CLUSTER_ID" --db-cluster-snapshot-identifier "$CLUSTER_ID-pre-encryption" --region "$REGION" && aws rds wait db-cluster-snapshot-available --db-cluster-snapshot-identifier "$CLUSTER_ID-pre-encryption" --region "$REGION" && aws rds copy-db-cluster-snapshot --source-db-cluster-snapshot-identifier "$CLUSTER_ID-pre-encryption" --target-db-cluster-snapshot-identifier "$CLUSTER_ID-encrypted" --kms-key-id "$KMS_KEY_ID" --region "$REGION" && aws rds wait db-cluster-snapshot-available --db-cluster-snapshot-identifier "$CLUSTER_ID-encrypted" --region "$REGION" && aws rds restore-db-cluster-from-snapshot --db-cluster-identifier "$NEW_CLUSTER_ID" --snapshot-identifier "$CLUSTER_ID-encrypted" --engine "$ENGINE" --db-subnet-group-name "$SUBNET_GROUP" --vpc-security-group-ids "$SG_ID" --db-cluster-parameter-group-name "$CLUSTER_PARAM_GROUP" --region "$REGION" && aws rds create-db-instance --db-instance-identifier "$NEW_CLUSTER_ID-1" --db-cluster-identifier "$NEW_CLUSTER_ID" --db-instance-class "$INSTANCE_CLASS" --engine "$ENGINE" --db-parameter-group-name "$PARAM_GROUP" --no-publicly-accessible --region "$REGION"
remediation.notes: It is a replacement, not an in-place change: RDS does not encrypt an existing database. Downtime: from stopping the application writes (a required step BEFORE the snapshot) until the endpoint switch; to shorten it, use DMS / a logical replica to sync the last stretch. Writes made after the snapshot are lost, which is why the application must not write between the snapshot and the switch. While the migration lasts, two databases are paid for. The first block is for an instance and the second one only for Aurora; a Multi-AZ DB cluster (not Aurora) is restored with restore-db-cluster-from-snapshot and --db-cluster-instance-class (see the steps), with no commands here. Parameter groups are passed explicitly (PARAM_GROUP, CLUSTER_PARAM_GROUP) and the instance's option group too (OPTION_GROUP): option groups are not inherited by restore-db-instance-from-db-snapshot. The restored database does not inherit Multi-AZ, read replicas, tags, backup retention, IAM auth, deletion protection, automatic minor version upgrade, log export to CloudWatch or the maintenance window: reconfigure them. Public access is not inherited either: RDS decides it by the subnet group (a subnet group with a route to an internet gateway gives a public database), which is why the blocks pass --no-publicly-accessible so that the replacement is not more exposed than the original (NET-007); if the original was public on purpose, change it explicitly after restoring. Verify with the command below (scoped to this database's identifier): an empty list means that no database keeps that identifier (for example the new one ended up with another name): query by the new identifier. Snapshots and replicas of an encrypted database stay encrypted. Do not delete the original database until the new one is validated.

checks.title: EFS file systems are encrypted at rest

verify.pass_when_text: All file systems have Encrypted=true. Encryption is decided when the file system is created and cannot be turned on afterwards (Drata 231 treats it the same way).

steps: Choose the KMS key (the default EFS one or your own CMK) and a maintenance window: the data in {resource_id} must be migrated to a new file system.

Create a new EFS file system with --encrypted in region {region} (the first block copies the original's performance mode and throughput mode, including provisioned throughput, which cannot be changed afterwards for the performance mode), with the same mount targets, security groups and backup policy.
Copy the data from the old file system to the new one with AWS DataSync (or rsync from an instance that mounts both).
Stop the writers, do a final sync and mount the new file system in the applications.
Verify the data and only then delete the unencrypted file system.
commands:
REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
OLD_FS_ID="{resource_id}"
TOKEN="encrypted-efs-$(date +%s)"
KMS_KEY_ID="__FILL_IN_KMS_KEY_ID__"
FS_NAME="__FILL_IN_FILE_SYSTEM_NAME__"
# performance mode (it cannot be changed later) and throughput mode of the original, read-only
PERF_MODE=$(aws efs describe-file-systems --file-system-id "$OLD_FS_ID" --region "$REGION" --query 'FileSystems[0].PerformanceMode' --output text) || PERF_MODE="READ_FAILED"
THR_MODE=$(aws efs describe-file-systems --file-system-id "$OLD_FS_ID" --region "$REGION" --query 'FileSystems[0].ThroughputMode' --output text) || THR_MODE="READ_FAILED"
PROV_THR=$(aws efs describe-file-systems --file-system-id "$OLD_FS_ID" --region "$REGION" --query 'FileSystems[0].ProvisionedThroughputInMibps' --output text) || PROV_THR="READ_FAILED"
THR_ARGS="--throughput-mode $THR_MODE"; [ "$THR_MODE" = "provisioned" ] && THR_ARGS="$THR_ARGS --provisioned-throughput-in-mibps $PROV_THR"
if [ "$PERF_MODE" = "READ_FAILED" ] || [ "$THR_MODE" = "READ_FAILED" ] || [ "$PROV_THR" = "READ_FAILED" ]; then echo "STOPPED: could not read the file system (elasticfilesystem:DescribeFileSystems); nothing was created"; else aws efs create-file-system --creation-token "$TOKEN" --encrypted --kms-key-id "$KMS_KEY_ID" --performance-mode "$PERF_MODE" $THR_ARGS --tags "Key=Name,Value=$FS_NAME" --region "$REGION"; fi

REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
NEW_FS_ID="__FILL_IN_NEW_FILE_SYSTEM_ID__"
SUBNET_ID="__FILL_IN_SUBNET_ID__"
SG_ID="__FILL_IN_SECURITY_GROUP_ID__"
# one per Availability Zone in which the file system is mounted
aws efs create-mount-target --file-system-id "$NEW_FS_ID" --subnet-id "$SUBNET_ID" --security-groups "$SG_ID" --region "$REGION"
remediation.notes: The first block creates the new file system with the same performance mode and throughput mode as the original (the performance mode cannot be changed later). Encryption cannot be turned on for an existing file system: a new one must be created and the data migrated. Downtime: that of the final sync and the remount in the applications. While the copy lasts, both file systems are paid for. Reapply the lifecycle policy, backup policy, access points and file system policy on the new one. With AWS Backup, restoring to a new file system also lets you choose encryption.

checks.title: S3 buckets have default encryption configured

verify.pass_when_text: Each bucket returns a default encryption rule (SSE-S3, SSE-KMS or DSSE-KMS). A bucket without a configuration (ServerSideEncryptionConfigurationNotFoundError) fails. Drata 69 accepts SSE-S3.

drata.name: Customer Data in Cloud Storage is Encrypted at Rest

steps: Configure default encryption on bucket {resource_id} with SSE-S3 (AES256), or with SSE-KMS if you need to control the key.
Verify with get-bucket-encryption.
commands:
REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
aws s3api put-bucket-encryption --bucket "{resource_id}" --server-side-encryption-configuration '{"Rules":[{"ApplyServerSideEncryptionByDefault":{"SSEAlgorithm":"AES256"}}]}'
remediation.notes: No downtime. It only affects new objects; existing ones are re-encrypted by copying them onto themselves or with S3 Batch Operations. For SSE-KMS use SSEAlgorithm=aws:kms with KMSMasterKeyID and BucketKeyEnabled=true (reduces KMS calls). put-bucket-encryption replaces the previous configuration: do not use it on a bucket that already has SSE-KMS.

checks.title: Symmetric customer-managed KMS keys have automatic rotation enabled

verify.pass_when_text: Every enabled, customer-managed, symmetric key with KMS key material has KeyRotationEnabled=true. AWS-managed keys (aws/* aliases), asymmetric keys, disabled keys, keys pending deletion and external-material keys do not apply. If a key's key policy blocks the auditor (as Drata 223 asks, the policy must allow kms:DescribeKey and kms:GetKeyRotationStatus), that key ends up NOT_VERIFIED with the missing permission and the others are evaluated.

vanta.test: Rotation is enabled for customer-created symmetric KMS keys

steps: Enable automatic rotation of key {resource_id} (by default, once a year).
Verify with get-key-rotation-status.
commands:
REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
aws kms enable-key-rotation --key-id "{resource_id}" --region "$REGION"
remediation.notes: No downtime and no re-encryption of data: KMS keeps the previous material to decrypt what is already encrypted and uses the new one for what is encrypted from now on. Each accumulated rotation can carry an additional monthly charge. With the recent CLI the period can be set with --rotation-period-in-days (90 to 2560, default 365). Keys from another account or with a closed key policy are fixed from the owning account.

checks.title: KMS keys are not scheduled for deletion

verify.pass_when_text: No key is in the PendingDeletion (or PendingReplicaDeletion) state. Deleting a key leaves the data encrypted with it unreadable forever. A key deleted between listing and querying does not apply; a key whose key policy blocks the auditor ends up NOT_VERIFIED.

steps: Confirm with the owning team whether key {resource_id} still encrypts data or resources (S3, EBS, RDS, secrets, trails).
If it is needed, cancel the deletion: cancel-key-deletion leaves the key disabled, so it must be enabled again.
If it is no longer needed, do nothing: it is deleted on the scheduled date and the data encrypted with it is lost.
commands:
REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
aws kms describe-key --key-id "{resource_id}" --region "$REGION" --query 'KeyMetadata.[KeyId,KeyState,DeletionDate,Description]'

REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
# only if the key is needed: cancels the deletion and enables it again
aws kms cancel-key-deletion --key-id "{resource_id}" --region "$REGION" && aws kms enable-key --key-id "{resource_id}" --region "$REGION"
remediation.notes: Decision: cancel or let it be deleted. While the key is pending deletion nobody can use it; if there are resources that depend on it, they are already failing. If the key is multi-Region, also check the replicas. For the intentional case (key retired on purpose), document the decision: this finding will keep appearing until the waiting period passes.

checks.title: Secrets Manager secrets have automatic rotation enabled

verify.pass_when_text: All secrets have RotationEnabled=true. Secrets scheduled for deletion are not included (list-secrets omits them).

steps: Decide whether secret {resource_id} can be rotated automatically: database secrets can (there are template rotation functions); a third party's API key is usually rotated by hand.
Have the rotation Lambda function (AWS template for the database engine) and confirm that its network reaches the database and Secrets Manager.
Enable rotation with a 90-day period and verify that the first rotation finishes successfully.
commands:
REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
ROTATION_LAMBDA_ARN="__FILL_IN_ROTATION_LAMBDA_ARN__"
aws secretsmanager rotate-secret --secret-id "{resource_id}" --rotation-lambda-arn "$ROTATION_LAMBDA_ARN" --rotation-rules AutomaticallyAfterDays=90 --region "$REGION"
remediation.notes: Decision: rotation function and period (90 days here). rotate-secret rotates once immediately (to disable that, add --no-rotate-immediately): applications must re-read the secret and tolerate the change of value, and if the function fails the secret does not change but the finding persists. Secrets that cannot be rotated (third-party keys) should be documented as an exception. Secrets managed by another service (for example the RDS master password) are rotated from that service.

checks.title: S3 buckets deny requests without TLS (aws:SecureTransport=false)

verify.pass_when_text: The bucket policy has an explicit Deny for all principals and S3 actions, with the condition Bool aws:SecureTransport=false (and no other), on the bucket and on its objects. A bucket without a policy (NoSuchBucketPolicy) fails, as in Drata 234.

steps: Fetch the current policy of bucket {resource_id} into a file (first block, read-only): if the bucket has no policy it starts from an empty one; on any other error (for example AccessDenied) it stops.

Add the aws:SecureTransport=false Deny statement to the file (second block, applies nothing) and review it: the Deny also cuts off clients that access over HTTP (old tools, http:// URLs in configurations, S3 websites).
Apply the reviewed policy with put-bucket-policy (third block) and verify with get-bucket-policy.
commands:
REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
BUCKET="{resource_id}"
# read-only: fetches the current policy into a file and shows it. If the bucket has no policy, it writes an empty one; on any other error (for example AccessDenied) it deletes the file and stops, and the second block cannot continue
rm -f "policy-$BUCKET-new.json"
if aws s3api get-bucket-policy --bucket "$BUCKET" --query Policy --output text > "policy-$BUCKET.json" 2> "policy-$BUCKET.err"; then cat "policy-$BUCKET.json"; elif grep -q NoSuchBucketPolicy "policy-$BUCKET.err"; then echo '{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[]}' > "policy-$BUCKET.json"; echo "the bucket has no policy: starting from an empty one"; else cat "policy-$BUCKET.err"; rm -f "policy-$BUCKET.json"; echo "STOPPED: could not read the current policy; do not continue"; fi

REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
BUCKET="{resource_id}"
# applies nothing: adds the Deny to the policy that was read (keeps all statements) and shows the result for review
rm -f "policy-$BUCKET-new.json"
if [ ! -s "policy-$BUCKET.json" ]; then echo "STOPPED: policy-$BUCKET.json is missing; run the first block first"; else python3 -c 'import json,sys; b=sys.argv[1]; p=json.load(open("policy-"+b+".json")); s=p.get("Statement",[]); s=[s] if isinstance(s,dict) else s; s.append({"Sid":"DenyInsecureTransport","Effect":"Deny","Principal":"*","Action":"s3:*","Resource":["arn:aws:s3:::"+b,"arn:aws:s3:::"+b+"/*"],"Condition":{"Bool":{"aws:SecureTransport":"false"}}}) if not any(isinstance(x,dict) and x.get("Sid")=="DenyInsecureTransport" for x in s) else None; p["Statement"]=s; json.dump(p,open("policy-"+b+"-new.json","w"),indent=2)' "$BUCKET" && cat "policy-$BUCKET-new.json"; fi

REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
BUCKET="{resource_id}"
# put-bucket-policy REPLACES the whole policy: apply only the reviewed file (policy-$BUCKET-new.json), never a hand-written policy
if [ -s "policy-$BUCKET-new.json" ]; then aws s3api put-bucket-policy --bucket "$BUCKET" --policy "file://policy-$BUCKET-new.json"; else echo "STOPPED: policy-$BUCKET-new.json is missing; run the previous blocks first"; fi
remediation.notes: put-bucket-policy replaces the entire policy: apply only the reviewed file that keeps the existing statements. If the bucket already has a policy (for example the CloudFront/OAC one of a site), the first block fetches it and the second only adds the Deny to it: a policy is never written from scratch over an existing one, and on a read error the fix stops with STOPPED. Decision: confirm that no legitimate client uses HTTP. A bucket with S3 website hosting only serves HTTP: do not apply the Deny there and put CloudFront (HTTPS) in front. CloudFront and AWS services talk to S3 over HTTPS and are not affected. The temporary files carry the bucket name (policy-<bucket>.json and policy-<bucket>-new.json) so as not to apply another bucket's by mistake; if the policy already has a statement with Sid DenyInsecureTransport the command does not add another, so check that this statement complies. The commands use python3, which CloudShell has installed.

checks.title: HTTP listeners of Application Load Balancers redirect to HTTPS

verify.pass_when_text: Every ALB HTTP listener has as its default action a redirect to HTTPS, port 443, with 301 or 302 (Drata 299). An ALB without HTTP listeners passes. Only the listener's default action is evaluated; the listener's rules are not. Network and gateway load balancers do not apply.

drata.name: AWS Application Load Balancer Redirects HTTP to HTTPS

steps: Confirm that load balancer {resource_id} already has an HTTPS:443 listener with a certificate and that its security group allows port 443 (the command stops with STOPPED if there is no HTTPS:443 listener).
Change the default action of the HTTP listeners to a permanent (301) redirect to HTTPS:443.
Verify that http://domain answers 301 to https://domain.
commands:
REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
LB_NAME="{resource_id}"
# it only redirects if the load balancer has an HTTPS listener on port 443; if not (or if it could not be read), it stops without changing anything
LB_ARN=$(aws elbv2 describe-load-balancers --names "$LB_NAME" --region "$REGION" --query 'LoadBalancers[0].LoadBalancerArn' --output text)
HTTPS_443=$(aws elbv2 describe-listeners --load-balancer-arn "$LB_ARN" --region "$REGION" --query 'length(Listeners[?Protocol==`HTTPS` && Port==`443`])' --output text)
case "$HTTPS_443" in
  ""|0|None) echo "STOPPED: the load balancer has no HTTPS:443 listener (or it could not be read): the redirect would leave the site inaccessible; create it first (ACM certificate, see TLS-005)";;
  *) for LISTENER_ARN in $(aws elbv2 describe-listeners --load-balancer-arn "$LB_ARN" --region "$REGION" --query 'Listeners[?Protocol==`HTTP`].ListenerArn' --output text); do aws elbv2 modify-listener --listener-arn "$LISTENER_ARN" --default-actions 'Type=redirect,RedirectConfig={Protocol=HTTPS,Port=443,StatusCode=HTTP_301}' --region "$REGION"; done;;
esac
remediation.verify_after: aws elbv2 describe-listeners --load-balancer-arn "$(aws elbv2 describe-load-balancers --names "{resource_id}" --region "{region}" --query 'LoadBalancers[0].LoadBalancerArn' --output text)" --region "{region}" --query 'Listeners[?Protocol==`HTTP`].DefaultActions[].RedirectConfig'
remediation.notes: Risk: without an HTTPS:443 listener the redirect would leave the site inaccessible, so the command checks it first and stops with STOPPED (changing nothing) if it does not exist or could not be read; create it first (ACM certificate, see TLS-005). With the listener present there is no downtime. The loop changes all HTTP listeners; if one serves internal traffic that must stay on HTTP, apply modify-listener only to the chosen listener's ARN. Clients that use HTTP receive a 301 and must follow it; the target groups' health checks are not affected. Only the listener's default action is evaluated and changed: the listener's rules are neither touched nor reviewed.

checks.title: HTTPS listeners of Application Load Balancers use a TLS 1.2 or higher policy

verify.pass_when_text: Every ALB HTTPS listener uses a policy that rejects TLS 1.0 and 1.1: ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-* (recommended: ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-2021-06), TLS13-1-3-*, FS-1-2-* or TLS-1-2-*. TLS13-1-1 and TLS13-1-0, FS-1-1, FS-2018-06, TLS-1-1 and TLS-1-0, 2016-08 (allows TLS 1.0), 2015-05 and any name that is not recognized fail.

steps: Change the policy of the HTTPS listeners of load balancer {resource_id} to ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-2021-06.
Verify with describe-listeners that SslPolicy has the new policy and test the oldest clients.
commands:
REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
LB_NAME="{resource_id}"
POLICY="ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-2021-06"
LB_ARN=$(aws elbv2 describe-load-balancers --names "$LB_NAME" --region "$REGION" --query 'LoadBalancers[0].LoadBalancerArn' --output text) && for LISTENER_ARN in $(aws elbv2 describe-listeners --load-balancer-arn "$LB_ARN" --region "$REGION" --query 'Listeners[?Protocol==`HTTPS`].ListenerArn' --output text); do aws elbv2 modify-listener --listener-arn "$LISTENER_ARN" --ssl-policy "$POLICY" --region "$REGION"; done
remediation.verify_after: aws elbv2 describe-listeners --load-balancer-arn "$(aws elbv2 describe-load-balancers --names "{resource_id}" --region "{region}" --query 'LoadBalancers[0].LoadBalancerArn' --output text)" --region "{region}" --query 'Listeners[?Protocol==`HTTPS`].[Port,SslPolicy]'
remediation.notes: Risk: no downtime, but clients that only speak TLS 1.0 or 1.1 (very old browsers and SDKs, some devices) can no longer connect: check the ALB access logs (ssl_protocol field) before changing. ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-2021-06 accepts TLS 1.2 and 1.3; the -Res- or -Ext- variants adjust the ciphers. The command changes all HTTPS listeners of the load balancer.

checks.title: RDS databases force the use of SSL/TLS (rds.force_ssl=1 or require_secure_transport=ON)

verify.pass_when_text: The instance's parameter group (or the cluster's, for Aurora and Multi-AZ DB cluster) has rds.force_ssl=1 (PostgreSQL, Aurora PostgreSQL, SQL Server) or require_secure_transport=ON (MySQL, MariaDB, Aurora MySQL). Engines without that parameter (Oracle, Db2) do not apply. default.* parameter groups cannot be modified, so a database that uses them only passes if the default value already forces SSL.

steps: Identify the parameter group of {resource_id} (finding detail.parameter_group). default.* ones cannot be modified: the blocks copy the current group (so the existing custom parameters are kept) and turn on SSL in the copy. Editing your own group directly is an alternative only if no other database uses it.

Copy the current parameter group, set rds.force_ssl=1 (PostgreSQL, SQL Server) or require_secure_transport=ON (MySQL, MariaDB) in the copy and associate the copy with the database or cluster (first block for an instance, second for a cluster).
Confirm that all applications already connect with SSL/TLS (for example sslmode=require) before rebooting, because afterwards connections without SSL are rejected.
Reboot the database in the maintenance window so that the new group is applied (third block; on a cluster it reboots each member) and check that connections keep working.
commands:
REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
DB_ID="{resource_id}"
SOURCE_PG="__FILL_IN_CURRENT_PARAMETER_GROUP_NAME__"
PG_NAME="__FILL_IN_NEW_PARAMETER_GROUP_NAME__"
# PostgreSQL and SQL Server: rds.force_ssl=1. MySQL and MariaDB: SSL_PARAM="require_secure_transport" and SSL_VALUE="ON"
SSL_PARAM="rds.force_ssl"
SSL_VALUE="1"
# instance that does not belong to a cluster; SOURCE_PG is its current group (detail.parameter_group): copying it keeps the custom parameters it already has. WARNING: --apply-immediately also applies any other pending change on the instance
aws rds copy-db-parameter-group --source-db-parameter-group-identifier "$SOURCE_PG" --target-db-parameter-group-identifier "$PG_NAME" --target-db-parameter-group-description "SSL required" --region "$REGION" && aws rds modify-db-parameter-group --db-parameter-group-name "$PG_NAME" --parameters "ParameterName=$SSL_PARAM,ParameterValue=$SSL_VALUE,ApplyMethod=pending-reboot" --region "$REGION" && aws rds modify-db-instance --db-instance-identifier "$DB_ID" --db-parameter-group-name "$PG_NAME" --apply-immediately --region "$REGION"

REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
CLUSTER_ID="{resource_id}"
SOURCE_PG="__FILL_IN_CURRENT_CLUSTER_PARAMETER_GROUP_NAME__"
PG_NAME="__FILL_IN_NEW_CLUSTER_PARAMETER_GROUP_NAME__"
# PostgreSQL and SQL Server: rds.force_ssl=1. MySQL and MariaDB: SSL_PARAM="require_secure_transport" and SSL_VALUE="ON"
SSL_PARAM="rds.force_ssl"
SSL_VALUE="1"
# cluster (Aurora or Multi-AZ DB cluster): the parameter lives in the cluster parameter group; SOURCE_PG is the cluster's current group (detail.parameter_group). WARNING: --apply-immediately also applies any other pending change on the cluster
aws rds copy-db-cluster-parameter-group --source-db-cluster-parameter-group-identifier "$SOURCE_PG" --target-db-cluster-parameter-group-identifier "$PG_NAME" --target-db-cluster-parameter-group-description "SSL required" --region "$REGION" && aws rds modify-db-cluster-parameter-group --db-cluster-parameter-group-name "$PG_NAME" --parameters "ParameterName=$SSL_PARAM,ParameterValue=$SSL_VALUE,ApplyMethod=pending-reboot" --region "$REGION" && aws rds modify-db-cluster --db-cluster-identifier "$CLUSTER_ID" --db-cluster-parameter-group-name "$PG_NAME" --apply-immediately --region "$REGION"

REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
DB_ID="{resource_id}"
# in the maintenance window: it interrupts connections. {resource_id} is an instance identifier or a cluster identifier: for a cluster it reboots each member, one after another, waiting for each to be available (readers first is safer: reboot the writer by hand last)
if aws rds describe-db-instances --db-instance-identifier "$DB_ID" --region "$REGION" > /dev/null 2>&1; then aws rds reboot-db-instance --db-instance-identifier "$DB_ID" --region "$REGION"; else for MEMBER in $(aws rds describe-db-clusters --db-cluster-identifier "$DB_ID" --region "$REGION" --query 'DBClusters[0].DBClusterMembers[].DBInstanceIdentifier' --output text); do aws rds reboot-db-instance --db-instance-identifier "$MEMBER" --region "$REGION" && aws rds wait db-instance-available --db-instance-identifier "$MEMBER" --region "$REGION"; done; fi
remediation.verify_after:
aws rds describe-db-parameters --db-parameter-group-name "$(aws rds describe-db-instances --db-instance-identifier "{resource_id}" --region "{region}" --query 'DBInstances[0].DBParameterGroups[0].DBParameterGroupName' --output text)" --region "{region}" --query 'Parameters[?ParameterName==`rds.force_ssl` || ParameterName==`require_secure_transport`].[ParameterName,ParameterValue]' # instance
aws rds describe-db-cluster-parameters --db-cluster-parameter-group-name "$(aws rds describe-db-clusters --db-cluster-identifier "{resource_id}" --region "{region}" --query 'DBClusters[0].DBClusterParameterGroup' --output text)" --region "{region}" --query 'Parameters[?ParameterName==`rds.force_ssl` || ParameterName==`require_secure_transport`].[ParameterName,ParameterValue]' # cluster: run this one instead when {resource_id} is a cluster identifier
remediation.notes: There is downtime: the reboot cuts connections (in Multi-AZ, a failover). Forcing SSL rejects any application, tool or job that connects without SSL: survey the connections beforehand and test in staging. ApplyMethod=pending-reboot works for static and dynamic parameters. The blocks copy the current parameter group instead of creating a blank one, so the custom parameters (timezone, binlog_format, etc.) are kept. --apply-immediately also applies any other pending change on the instance or cluster: check describe-db-instances / describe-db-clusters (PendingModifiedValues) first. On engines without rds.force_ssl support (Oracle), encryption in transit is configured with option group options, which this check does not evaluate. On a new database it is advisable to create the own parameter group from the start.

checks.title: ACM certificates have more than 30 days of validity left

verify.pass_when_text: Each issued certificate has MORE than 30 days until its NotAfter; with exactly 30 days or fewer it fails (the comparison is in exact seconds). Certificates that were never issued (pending validation or failed) do not apply. It does not cover the server certificates stored in IAM, which is what the cited Vanta test measures: check them with aws iam list-server-certificates.

steps: Check the status and type of certificate {resource_id}: those issued by ACM with DNS validation renew themselves as long as the validation CNAME record remains in DNS.
If it is an ACM certificate that is not renewing, restore the validation CNAME record or request a new certificate with DNS validation.
If it is an imported certificate, obtain the renewed certificate and re-import it over the same ARN: the listeners and resources that use it do not change.
If a new certificate was requested, associate it with the listeners and resources that used the old one and verify the new expiry with describe-certificate.
commands:
REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
aws acm describe-certificate --certificate-arn "{resource_id}" --region "$REGION" --query 'Certificate.[Status,Type,RenewalEligibility,RenewalSummary.RenewalStatus,NotAfter,InUseBy]'

REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
CERT_ARN="{resource_id}"
CERT_FILE="__FILL_IN_CERTIFICATE_FILE__"
KEY_FILE="__FILL_IN_PRIVATE_KEY_FILE__"
CHAIN_FILE="__FILL_IN_CHAIN_FILE__"
# only for imported certificates: re-imports over the same ARN
aws acm import-certificate --certificate-arn "$CERT_ARN" --certificate "fileb://$CERT_FILE" --private-key "fileb://$KEY_FILE" --certificate-chain "fileb://$CHAIN_FILE" --region "$REGION"

REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
DOMAIN="__FILL_IN_DOMAIN__"
# only for ACM certificates that are not renewing: requests a new one; then create the CNAME shown by describe-certificate
aws acm request-certificate --domain-name "$DOMAIN" --validation-method DNS --region "$REGION"
remediation.notes: No downtime if it is re-imported over the same ARN or if the certificate is switched on the listeners with the new one already issued. ACM renews its own certificates roughly 60 days before expiry: an ACM certificate with fewer than 30 days left usually has broken validation. Imported certificates do not renew themselves. A private key is never pasted into the console or a ticket: it is read from the file in CloudShell. Server certificates stored in IAM (Vanta: Expired SSL/TLS certificates are removed from IAM) are not evaluated by this check: list them with aws iam list-server-certificates and delete expired ones with delete-server-certificate.
